content: Trachoma is an infectious eye disease and is recognized as the leading cause of preventable blindness worldwide. The disease is caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis. It is transmitted through direct contact with eye, nose, or throat secretions from infected individuals. Additionally, it can spread via fomites, which are inanimate objects such as towels or washcloths that have come into contact with these secretions. During a physical examination, an eye exam may reveal scarring on the inner surface of the upper eyelid, redness of the sclera (the white part of the eyes), and the growth of new blood vessels into the cornea, a condition known as corneal neovascularization. Treatment involves the use of antibiotics, which, if administered early in the course of the infection, can prevent long-term complications. Commonly used antibiotics include erythromycin and doxycycline. In some cases, surgical intervention on the eyelid may be necessary to prevent severe scarring, which, if left untreated, can lead to blindness. Trachoma has a significant global impact, affecting 84 million people with active infections and leaving nearly 8 million individuals visually impaired. This disease results in an estimated $9 billion in lost productivity annually.
